chapters.title: One cap, one contingency rule
chapters.intro: This book is a kitchen planning roadmap for compact US homes and rentals. It is not a building-code manual, an electrical or gas guide, a plumbing license, a structural design, or legal advice. Some scenarios use apartments in Indian cities as compact-space illustrations. They do not define the market. Prices are in US dollars. Measurements are in inches. Example dollar amounts are illustrations, not typical remodel prices. 1 inch equals 25 mm if you need a conversion. Manufacturer instructions, the lease, building rules, licensed trades, and the authority having jurisdiction take precedence. You may plan, measure, document, and photograph. Qualified professionals perform electrical, gas, structural, and permit-required plumbing work. A score, a heat map, or a contingency formula in this book does not authorize unsafe work. Contingency lives inside the budget cap. It is not added on top. There is one method in this book. Ignore older notes that used a separate 8 percent plus risk-score formula, a competing 10–12 percent band, or a 12–15 percent band as a second calculator.

sections.principle: Write the cap first. A cosmetic refresh and a systems remodel are different projects.
body: Today's output: a written kitchen cap in USD, labeled illustrative until you have local quotes, plus three buckets — must have, should have, will not do.

Dollar figures in this book are planning scenarios. Actual cost varies by city, labor, appliances, existing conditions, and whether a qualified person must open walls. A small paint-and-hardware refresh is not the same budget as moving plumbing or electrical.

State whether the cap includes professional labor, materials, permits, waste, and contingency. If labor is extra, write that. Weekly budget review (the old notes said CFO review — that is a metaphor, not a job title) starts after this page exists.

sections.scenario: Kitchen measurement error: two formulas on the same sheet produced two different leftover amounts.
sections.principle: Reserve twelve percent of the cap as contingency. Cut other lines if risk is high. Do not add contingency on top of the cap.
body: Today's output: the same cap, with working cost at eighty-eight percent and contingency at twelve percent, summing to one hundred percent of the cap. Category lines under working cost must add up to the working-cost total. Contingency is not copied into those categories.

Worked illustration, not a quote: cap 10,000 USD. Working cost 8,800 USD. Contingency reserved 1,200 USD. Example cosmetic split of the 8,800: demolition and waste 900, qualified fixture electrical or plumbing 2,000, finishes 2,200, fixtures 2,400, permits and fees 600, tools 700. Those six lines equal 8,800. Plus 1,200 reserved equals the cap. Do not also add 10–12 percent on top.

People overrun 15–25 percent when they have no cap and they spend the reserve during planning. Contingency is not a forecast of that overrun. If unknowns are high (old plumbing, moisture, complex permits), rescope first. If you still proceed, raise the reserved percent only by reducing other categories so the cap does not move. Do not use 8 percent plus half a percent times a risk score.

chapters.title: Renters, buildings, and local rules
chapters.intro: Permit requirements vary by jurisdiction and project scope. Building-owner or association approval may be required even when a municipal permit is not. Electrical, gas, structural, and plumbing work must be assessed against applicable local requirements. This book is not a substitute for official approval or professional code interpretation. Load-bearing walls are not the only structural concern. Shared stacks, exhaust, waterproofing, and fire assemblies can be affected.

chapters.intro: A plug-in tester is not a full electrical inspection. Air at a hood grille is not proof of a legal exhaust system. Water-heater settings are not the same as tap temperature. Do not adjust a water heater just to chase a number from this book.

sections.title: Functional checks without false comfort

sections.scenario: Final punch-list discovery: a tissue 'passed' on a recirculating hood that never had a path outside.
sections.principle: Record what you observed. Do not certify the house.
body: Today's output: a test sheet that states limits. Hot water: comfort and scald risk depend on the system, local rules, and who uses the sink. Do not raise or lower the water heater yourself solely because a 120°F target was missed. Tap temperature is not the heater setting. Ask a qualified person if adjustment or replacement is needed.

Electrical: a plug-in tester can catch some wiring errors on that receptacle. It does not prove every safety condition. It does not replace required inspection. Stop on suspected faults, heat, damage, or missing protection — Day 8.

Ventilation: kitchen exhaust is not a bathroom fan. Recirculating hoods filter and return air; they are not ducted exhaust. Airflow at the grille does not prove duct route, discharge, or required performance. Check the installed type against the plan and the manufacturer's instructions.

Estimate at Completion means your current forecast of total cost if you continue as now. If that forecast exceeds the cap, rescope. The reserve is not a shopping fund.
